newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Holiday for a slain prince shows Burundi divide.
newsitem.headline: Holiday for a slain prince shows Burundi divide.

text.p: A murdered Tutsi prince, a partisan crowd and a bullet-proof jacket evoked Burundi's ethnic divide on Sunday.
Ceremonies marking the 35th anniversary of the assassination of Prince Louis Rwagasore, officially a national hero, fell victim to the fear and suspicion that haunt the country.
Armed presidential guards were inside and outside Bujumbura's Regina Mundi cathedral at the packed mass for Rwagasore, the closest Burundi has to a founding father.
Despite the heavy security, Major Pierre Buyoya, installed as president in a military coup last July 25, did not appear.

The appeal by the capital's mayor for Sunday's events to be apolitical were ignored by supporters of Uprona, the party that Rwagasore founded before independence and which today champions his Tutsi minority.
The "Upronistes" wore their red-and-white caps and shirts at the mass and later at the arched monument to the dead prince, high in the hills overlooking the city.

Buyoya laid the first wreath on the tomb to warm applause from the crowd of a few hundred. But booing broke out when Leonce Ngendakumana, his girth broadened by what appeared to be a bullet-proof jacket under his double-breasted suit, stepped up with a crown of flowers.
Ngendakumana, the speaker of parliament, was the senior representative at the ceremonies from Frodebu, Burundi's largest party and dominated by the Hutu majority.
Frodebu's green-and-white colours were not in evidence.

"There is a lot of suspicion about Leonce," said Adolphe Nahayo, a Uprona member of parliament. The speaker, heading a parliament itself decimated by assassinations, is under investigation by the attorney-general's office for alleged involvement in "genocide" against Tutsis in 1993.
"This national day should unite everyone but because of what is happening in Burundi those who are not Uprona, and particularly Hutus, do not feel involved," Nahayo told Reuters.

By all accounts that division would upset the prince, had he survived the bullets that a Greek called Kageorgis pumped into him at close range on the terrace of the Tanganyika restaurant on October 13, 1961.
Rwagasore, the son of the reigning Tutsi monarch, had just been appointed prime minister during the period of self- government before independence from Belgium in 1962.
He was fighting other forces, both local and colonial, who wanted freedom delayed by many years.
Two aristocratic Tutsis, the Baranyanka brothers, were found guilty of hiring Kageorgis as a hitman. All three were hanged at Gitega, the seat of Burundi's Tutsi king.
"The problems were already there but the assassination crystallised them," said Nahayo, a keen historian.
Burundi has known chapters of peace since the murder but ethnic massacres in 1972, 1988 and 1993 were the spasms that foreshadowed the great trauma it suffers today.
Amnesty International, the human rights organisation, says 150,000 Hutus and Tutsis in a population of only six million have met violent ends since 1993.
Buyoya is the fourth president since then, a product of the southern Tutsi elite that dominates the army and is fighting a guerrilla war with Hutu rebels.
Many date the present crisis to the murder of Melchior Ndadaye, Burundi's first freely elected president, by Tutsi soldiers who did not tolerate a Hutu head of state.
Ndadaye only survived as president for one Rwagasore anniversary and he boycotted it on the grounds that the event had become political.
On October 21, in another national holiday for a slain leader, Burundi will mark the third anniversary of Ndadaye's assassination.
